solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Excellent vehicle brought into road for series of events (8)

indicators.note: the vehicle words are brought inside the road abbreviation

blocks.note: RD is the standard abbreviation for road; it opens around the rest

annotation.surface: A smart car is driven onto a road for some kind of event programme.
annotation.walkthrough: A racecard is the printed programme listing a day's races at a racecourse, which is why it counts as a series of events.
annotation.definitionFit: A racecard lists the sequence of races run at a meeting.

clue.text: Distance the writer picked up during journey (6)

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting ME up turns it round to EM
EM sits during, i.e. inside, the journey word

blocks.note: to rove is to journey or wander; it goes around EM
the writer = the setter, ME; reversed to EM

annotation.surface: A travel writer measures how far they have come on a trip.
annotation.walkthrough: The noun remove means a degree of distance, as in 'at one remove'; the verb sense is the obvious one and a trap here.
annotation.definitionFit: A remove is a step or degree of separation, as in 'at several removes from reality'.

clue.text: Stay calm, somehow, after onset of complete disaster (9)

indicators.note: the letters of STAY CALM are arranged somehow
the anagram comes after the C
the onset of a word is its first letter

annotation.surface: Advice to keep your head when total catastrophe begins.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a keep-calm slogan for a crisis, so the disaster in the answer belongs to the scene the clue paints.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a cataclysm is a sudden, violent upheaval, the worst kind of disaster.

clue.text: Gladden children, getting pulpy food served with a twist (5,2)

indicators.note: PUREE twisted round runs backwards as EERUP

blocks.note: CH is a standard abbreviation for children

blocks.clueFragment: pulpy food served with a twist

annotation.surface: Kids are cheered up with mashed food served in a fancy way.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a parent's trick at mealtimes; 'served' belongs to that picture and adds nothing to the mechanics.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as transitive verbs: both mean making someone feel happier.

clue.text: Reliable, not initially out of practice (5)

indicators.note: the initial letter is left off

blocks.note: TRUSTY (reliable) minus its first letter T

annotation.surface: Someone who used to be dependable has lost their edge through lack of practice.
annotation.walkthrough: The two halves seem to contradict each other: reliable, yet out of practice.
annotation.definitionFit: Skills that are rusty have weakened through lack of practice.

clue.text: Knave almost entirely a scoundrel (6)

indicators.note: almost the whole word: the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: the knave in a pack of cards is the jack

annotation.surface: A knave is described as more or less a total rogue.
annotation.walkthrough: Knave and scoundrel look like synonyms of each other, but the knave is the playing card; a jackal is someone who does another's dirty work.
annotation.definitionFit: A jackal is a person who does base or dishonest work for someone else.

clue.text: Article from soldier keeping Spain in suspense (7)

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so the soldier phrase holds the Spain letter inside it

blocks.note: from = by, as in a letter from or by someone; E goes inside
E is the international vehicle code for Spain

annotation.surface: An item written by a soldier who is stationed in Spain is left undecided.
annotation.walkthrough: 'From' means by, as in a gift from or by a friend; and the soldier is the soldier ant, a crossword favourite. 'In suspense' is the state of being held in abeyance.
annotation.definitionFit: Abeyant describes something held in abeyance, suspended or pending.

clue.text: Blade, if slicing joint, cut (5)

indicators.note: IF slices into the joint word
the result is cut short by one letter

blocks.note: the knee is a joint; IF goes inside after KN

annotation.surface: A butcher's instruction about using a blade on a joint of meat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Joint' suggests a joint of meat in the kitchen scene, but it is the body's knee.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by part: the blade is the business end of any knife, so the word stands for the whole tool.

clue.text: French are invading Scottish town, supported by English generosity (8)

indicators.note: an invader pushes into territory, so the French word pushes into the middle of the town
in a down clue, the E below supports what sits above

annotation.walkthrough: 'French are' is ES because the setter takes the form from 'tu es'; the English E at the foot of the down entry is the support.

blocks.note: Largs is a seaside town on the Firth of Clyde; ES goes inside

annotation.surface: The French invade a Scottish town and the English generously back them.
annotation.definitionFit: Largesse is generosity, especially in giving money or gifts.

clue.text: Question a wild speech about termination of third sector (8)

indicators.note: about means around, so the wild speech with its A wraps around the letter from third
a termination is an ending, so only the final letter of the word is used

blocks.note: QU is an abbreviation for question
a rant is a wild speech

annotation.surface: Someone challenges a wild speech about the end of the third sector, meaning charities.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'third sector' is the charity and voluntary sector, a phrase that pulls 'sector' into the surface rather than the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A geometric sense: a quarter of a circle is a sector cut by two radii at right angles.

clue.text: Thermos drunk, police officer heads to investigate oddly rowdy religious figures (7,8)

indicators.note: THERMOS is drunk, so its letters stagger into a new order
take the heads, the first letters, of the words that follow

blocks.note: first letters of investigate, oddly, rowdy

annotation.surface: A drunken flask, a policeman and a rowdy group of nuns under investigation.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' looks like an instruction to take alternate letters, but here it is only one of the three words whose heads are taken.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the heads of convents are one kind of religious figure among many.

clue.text: Former Queen only losing heart about reserve representative of her power (7)

indicators.note: ONLY loses its middle letters NL
VR and OY together go about ICE

blocks.note: Victoria Regina, Queen Victoria's royal cypher
ice = coolness or reserve of manner; goes inside

annotation.surface: A former queen, lacking courage, relies on a distant deputy for her authority.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Her' points back to the queen of the surface: a viceroy governs a colony in the monarch's name, as in British India.
annotation.definitionFit: A viceroy rules a territory as the sovereign's representative.

clue.text: Detective pursuing former marksman (7)

indicators.note: EYE comes after DEAD, pursuing it

blocks.note: a private eye is a detective

annotation.surface: A detective is on the trail of a one-time sharpshooter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Former' looks like it modifies 'marksman', but it supplies the first half; dead means no longer, as in a dead language.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, originally American: someone with a dead eye never misses a target.

clue.text: Rebuffed excellent concessions when hosting my conferences (8)

indicators.note: rebuffed means pushed back, so the whole is read backwards
a host has guests inside the house, so the concessions word holds MY inside it

blocks.note: A1 = excellent, the 1 read as I
sops are concessions to appease someone; MY goes inside before the last S

annotation.surface: Generous concessions are turned down when I host meetings.
annotation.walkthrough: A1 SOP(MY)S is assembled first and then read backwards; the 1 in A1 serves as the letter I.
annotation.definitionFit: Symposia is the plural of symposium, a conference.

clue.text: Wisdom, e.g., about way of walking round capital of Cuba (8)

indicators.note: SAY goes about the walking word
round means encircling, so the way of walking encircles the capital letter

blocks.note: say = for example; it surrounds the rest
your gait is your way of walking

annotation.surface: A wise remark about someone's walk around Havana.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capital of Cuba' wants to be Havana; it is only the capital letter C.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both name sound judgement, sagacity leaning towards shrewd practical sense.

clue.text: Literary heroine accepting first of two challenges (5)

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so the heroine takes the letter into her name
first of means the opening letter of the word that follows

annotation.walkthrough: 'Literary heroine' is a crossword stock phrase; Tess of the d'Urbervilles, Thomas Hardy's novel, supplies the name most often.

blocks.note: Tess of the d'Urbervilles, Thomas Hardy's heroine

annotation.surface: A heroine in a novel takes on the first of two ordeals.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as plural nouns: trials of ability or nerve.

clue.text: Old Queen, enthralled by very good flower, talking to herself? (9)

definitions.note: the definition is by example: a soliloquy is a speech made talking to oneself

indicators.note: O QU is held captive inside LILY

blocks.note: a lily is a flower; it holds O and QU
QU is an abbreviation for queen

annotation.surface: An old queen, charmed by a lovely flower, murmurs to herself.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Very good' looks like a single phrase, but 'very' is SO and 'good' is part of the surface. The question mark flags that 'herself' is just one example of the speaker.
annotation.definitionFit: A soliloquy is a speech in which a character talks to themselves.

clue.text: Develops source of some hard copies completely (6,2)

indicators.note: the source of a word is its first letter

annotation.surface: A photo lab develops some of the prints as hard copies.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is about developing film and printing, which hides that 'Develops' means progresses.
annotation.definitionFit: Something that shapes up develops, usually satisfactorily.

clue.text: Disheartened holy man’s offloading a songbook’s content (5)

indicators.note: HOLY loses its heart, the middle OL
to offload is to get rid of cargo, so the A is unloaded from the word

annotation.walkthrough: 'Disheartened' removes the heart of the word, its middle two letters, not a single letter.
annotation.surface: A dejected priest gives away the contents of his hymnal.
annotation.definitionFit: A hymn book's contents are hymns.

clue.text: Son less convincing about motive’s heading for prison (7)

indicators.note: about means around, so the less convincing word sits around the motive letter
the heading of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: a lame excuse is unconvincing; goes around M

annotation.surface: A son with an ever feebler story about why he did it is headed for jail.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a courtroom scene, so 'prison' at the end looks like the fate of the son rather than the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A slang sense: the slammer is prison, named for the door slammed shut on the inmate.

clue.text: Numbers attending church shown in large page (8)

blocks.note: the gate is the number of people attending a match
the fold is a church congregation, the flock

annotation.surface: Church attendance figures are printed on an oversized page.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Numbers attending' reads as churchgoers; it is the gate, the attendance at a sports event.
annotation.definitionFit: A gatefold is an oversized page folded into a book or magazine.

clue.text: Displays article from Paris in apartments (7)

indicators.note: in means inside, so the French article is placed inside the apartments

annotation.walkthrough: 'Article from Paris' means a French article, here the masculine un, not a piece of writing from a Paris paper.

blocks.note: flats are apartments; UN goes inside
un is the French indefinite article

annotation.surface: A Parisian magazine article is shown off in someone's apartment.
annotation.definitionFit: To flaunt something is to display it ostentatiously.

clue.text: Refuse to make building blocks? That’s a blow (6)

blocks.note: refuse here is the noun: cinders and ash, mixed with cement for lightweight blocks
a blow as in wind blowing: a light wind

annotation.surface: Someone refusing to build with blocks is told it's a setback.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like a verb meaning decline; it is the noun, rubbish. Breeze blocks are lightweight building blocks made of cinders and cement.
annotation.definitionFit: Breeze is small cinders used in blocks; a breeze is a wind that blows.

clue.text: Dull expert still offering no end to torment at all (7)

indicators.note: no Ts are allowed to remain
every T goes, not just one

blocks.clueFragment: still offering no end to torment at all
blocks.note: STATIC (still) with every T, the end letter of torment, removed

annotation.surface: A dull expert still keeps up the torment without end.
annotation.walkthrough: The end of torment is T, and 'at all' means both Ts in STATIC go, leaving SAIC.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: prosaic writing is as flat as prose, with no poetry in it.

clue.text: Forty-one kept in work producing flower (5)

indicators.note: something kept in stays inside, so the number stays inside the work abbreviation

annotation.walkthrough: 'Forty-one' is Roman numerals, XL for forty and I for one; OP, short for opus, is the usual crossword work.

blocks.note: OP = opus, a work; XLI goes inside

annotation.surface: Forty-one pieces of work combine to produce a flower.
annotation.definitionFit: The oxlip is a woodland flower related to the primrose and cowslip.

clue.text: Slow mover caught by fishing boat with no prow (7)

indicators.note: the prow is a boat's front, so the first letter goes

blocks.note: TRAWLER without its front letter T

annotation.surface: A slow creature is hauled up by a trawler that has lost its bow.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Caught' looks like the verb of the fishing scene; it is the cricket scorecard abbreviation C.
annotation.definitionFit: A crawler is something that moves slowly.

clue.text: Historic English family upheld story about Conservative clubs (5)

indicators.note: in a down clue, held up means read from the bottom
about means around, so the story wraps around the Conservative letter

blocks.note: a lie is a story; it goes around C

annotation.surface: An old English dynasty is backed by a tale about Tory clubs.
annotation.walkthrough: LI(C)E + C is built first, then the whole is read upwards. The Cecils are the family of Lord Burghley and the Marquesses of Salisbury, statesmen since Elizabeth I.
annotation.definitionFit: The Cecils are a long-standing English political family.

clue.text: Malta is implicated with dodgy cheque in fraudulent activity (6,9)

indicators.note: the letters are tangled up together
dodgy means unreliable, so the letters are not to be trusted in their order

annotation.surface: Malta is caught up in a scam involving a bad cheque.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link to the definition but it is needed in the fodder. A salami technique is fraud by skimming many tiny slices, such as fractions of pence from many accounts.
annotation.definitionFit: The salami technique is a fraud built from many small thefts that go unnoticed.

clue.text: Thin primate embraced by peer (6)

indicators.note: to be embraced is to be held in someone's arms, so the primate sits inside the other word

blocks.note: to peer is to pry, look closely; goes around APE

annotation.surface: A skinny monkey is hugged by a lord.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Peer' reads as a noble, but it is the verb, to look closely.
annotation.definitionFit: Papery means thin like paper.

clue.text: Interface of DOS and telly not the latest thing? (3,5)

indicators.note: DOS and TELLY are interfaced, merged so their letters mesh

blocks.note: anagram fodder; telly is British slang for television

annotation.surface: An old computer operating system hooked to a television is hardly cutting-edge.
annotation.walkthrough: DOS is an old computer operating system, so the surface is itself about out-of-date technology; 'and' only joins the two pieces of fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Something old-style is old-fashioned, the opposite of the latest thing.
